final_proof:
Let \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Write \(\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)\in\mathbb N_0^n\). For multiindices \(\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n)\), the notation \(0\leq\beta\leq\alpha\) means \(0\leq\beta_j\leq\alpha_j\) for every \(j\). Recall the standard definitions
\[
z^\gamma:=\prod_{j=1}^n z_j^{\gamma_j}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\binom{\alpha}{\beta}:=\prod_{j=1}^n\binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j}.
\]
Addition and subtraction of multiindices and tuples are componentwise. As usual for monomials, a zeroth power is \(1\).

By the ordinary binomial theorem, for each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\),
\[
(x_j+y_j)^{\alpha_j}
=\sum_{b_j=0}^{\alpha_j}
\binom{\alpha_j}{b_j}x_j^{b_j}y_j^{\alpha_j-b_j}.
\]
Consequently, using the definition of a multiindex power and then substituting these \(n\) identities,
\[
(x+y)^\alpha
=\prod_{j=1}^n(x_j+y_j)^{\alpha_j}
=\prod_{j=1}^n\left(\sum_{b_j=0}^{\alpha_j}
\binom{\alpha_j}{b_j}x_j^{b_j}y_j^{\alpha_j-b_j}\right).
\]
All these sums and products are finite. Repeated application of the distributive law expands the last expression by choosing, independently for every \(j\), one integer \(b_j\in\{0,\ldots,\alpha_j\}\). Such choices are in bijection with the multiindices \(\beta=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\) satisfying \(0\leq\beta\leq\alpha\). Hence
\[
(x+y)^\alpha
=\sum_{0\leq\beta\leq\alpha}
\prod_{j=1}^n\left(\binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j}
x_j^{\beta_j}y_j^{\alpha_j-\beta_j}\right).
\]
For each such \(\beta\), commutativity and associativity of multiplication in \(\mathbb R\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\prod_{j=1}^n\left(\binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j}
x_j^{\beta_j}y_j^{\alpha_j-\beta_j}\right)
&=\left(\prod_{j=1}^n\binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j}\right)
\left(\prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{\beta_j}\right)
\left(\prod_{j=1}^n y_j^{\alpha_j-\beta_j}\right)\\
&=\binom{\alpha}{\beta}x^\beta y^{\alpha-\beta}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution into the preceding sum yields
\[
\boxed{(x+y)^\alpha=\sum_{0\leq\beta\leq\alpha}
\binom{\alpha}{\beta}x^\beta y^{\alpha-\beta}},
\]
as required.
